holidays.name: National Hot Cross Bun Day
holidays.description: A day for tucking into spiced, fruit-studded buns marked with a sweet icing cross. Hot cross buns are usually tied to Easter and Good Friday, so having them in September is a bonus. Warm one up, add butter, and enjoy it out of season.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial food observance of unclear origin. It's a late-summer reminder that the beloved spiced bun doesn't need to wait for spring.
holidays.funFact: The buns have their own nursery rhyme, "Hot Cross Buns!" It's one of the first tunes many kids learn on the recorder, and it uses only three notes.

holidays.name: National Make Your Bed Day
holidays.description: An invitation to start the morning with one small win: pulling up the covers, fluffing the pillows, and smoothing out the sheets. It's a tiny act of tidiness that some people say sets a productive tone for the whole day. It also makes crawling back in at night feel a bit fancier.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It fits neatly into the back-to-routine mood of early September.
holidays.funFact: Retired U.S. Navy Admiral William McRaven made bed-making famous in a 2014 university commencement speech. He later turned it into a bestselling book called Make Your Bed.

holidays.name: No News is Good News Day
holidays.description: A day for taking a breather from the headlines and the constant scroll. Switch off the alerts, put the phone down, and enjoy some quiet. It's a reminder that sometimes silence really is golden.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It plays on the old proverb that no news means nothing bad has happened.
holidays.funFact: The proverb "no news is good news" goes back centuries. English writers were using it in the 1600s, and King James I is often credited with an early version.
